name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,704

clue.text: Hurry up and get big diaper on son

indicators.note: one thing placed on another here means the second piece is attached after the first

blocks.note: to make it is to become successful, to get big
S is the standard abbreviation for son
a nappy is the British word for a baby's diaper

explanation.surface: A parent is urged to be quick and put a large nappy on their little boy.
explanation.walkthrough: The son goes before the diaper, reading 'diaper on son' as S with NAPPY tacked on. A nappy is the British name for what Americans call a diaper.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiomatic command telling someone to be quick, the same urging as hurry up.

clue.text: Butch old lady sits on church official's head

indicators.note: in a down clue sitting on something means being placed above it, so earlier in the answer
the head of a word is its top, its opening letter

blocks.note: an old lady is slang for one's mother, MA
CH is the usual abbreviation for church
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A tough old woman perches on the head of a church dignitary.
explanation.walkthrough: Old lady is a slang term for mother, hence MA.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a showily tough, masculine manner, so they are near synonyms as adjectives.

clue.text: Immature beasts ruin child's play

blocks.note: kids are young goats
to stuff, in slang, is to wreck or defeat thoroughly

explanation.surface: Unruly young animals spoil the games of a youngster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Immature' suggests childish people, but the beasts are literal young goats.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are idioms for a task so simple that any youngster could manage it.

clue.text: Where liquor-drinking drunk might find solace briefly

definitions.text: Where liquor-drinking drunk might find solace

blocks.clueFragment: Where liquor-drinking drunk might find solace
blocks.note: first meaning, cryptic: a short is a small measure of spirits, so a drinker of liquor finds comfort inside one
second meaning: to sum up in few words

explanation.surface: A boozer seeks comfort in the bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: A short is a British term for a measure of spirits such as whisky or gin, as opposed to a long drink like beer.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an adverbial idiom used to sum something up concisely, matching the sense of briefly.

clue.text: Language so wantonly awful hussar is left incensed at front

indicators.note: only what sits at the front of each word is wanted, the opening letters

blocks.clueFragment: so wantonly awful hussar is left incensed
blocks.note: opening letters of seven consecutive words

explanation.surface: A cavalry soldier swears so foully that he leaves people furious.
explanation.walkthrough: A hussar is a light cavalry soldier; the long rambling surface hides an acrostic.
explanation.definitionFit: Swahili is a Bantu tongue widely spoken in East Africa, an example of a language.

clue.text: A criminal casing back of flat in London district

indicators.note: a casing wraps around its contents, so one piece encloses another
the back of a word is its end, so its final letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
a con is a convict, a criminal
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A burglar sizes up the rear of an apartment in a part of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Casing' looks like a thief's reconnaissance; here it means wrapping around. Acton is a district of west London.
explanation.definitionFit: Acton is a suburb in the west of the capital, an example of a city area there.

clue.text: Remarkable events men phone up about at summit

indicators.note: stirred up and turned about suggests letters thrown into a new order
a summit is the top, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Delegates at a summit call each other about extraordinary happenings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Summit' sounds like a diplomatic meeting, but it points to the top letter of 'at'. The rearranged words supply all but the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Phenomena are notable occurrences or marvels, the plural of phenomenon, so a synonym for remarkable events.

clue.text: Predatory flapper is cruel bride, Spooner said

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of neighbouring words

blocks.note: cruel is harsh; it takes the opening sound of the next word
a bride is one who marries; it takes the opening sound of the previous word

explanation.surface: A flighty young woman of the 1920s is a heartless bride, says Spooner.
explanation.walkthrough: A flapper looks like a 1920s party girl, but here it is anything that flaps its wings. The marsh harrier is a European bird of prey.
explanation.definitionFit: This raptor hunts over wetlands, so it is a bird that kills prey and flaps its wings.

clue.text: A reservation about rogue in galleries?

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: taken as written
RES is the common abbreviation for a reservation
a cad is a dishonourable man, a rogue

explanation.surface: Someone has misgivings about a scoundrel lurking in art galleries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reservation' reads as a doubt; it is the booking sense, abbreviated.
explanation.definitionFit: An arcade is a covered walkway lined with arches or shops, which is one sense of a gallery.

clue.text: Soldier cried briefly, having necked rare port

indicators.note: something said briefly is cut short, losing its final letter
to neck a drink is to gulp it down, taking something inside

blocks.note: a soldier ant is a kind of ant
to cry is to weep
R is an abbreviation for rare

explanation.surface: A soldier sobbed after downing some vintage port wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' seems to be the drink the soldier necked; it is the definition, a harbour city. Antwerp is a major Belgian seaport.
explanation.definitionFit: Antwerp is a city in Belgium with one of Europe's largest harbours, an example of a seaport.

clue.text: Don't give so many orgasms? That's no fun!

blocks.note: first meaning, cryptic: an instruction to provide less physical delight, split into two words
second meaning: lacking any enjoyment

explanation.surface: A cheeky complaint about a lover being told to hold back in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading splits the answer into a noun and a verb, telling someone to provide less delight.
explanation.definitionFit: Something without enjoyment is joyless, so an adjective meaning dull or no fun describes it.

clue.text: Drunks drinking drop of Caledonian?

definitions.note: the whole clue, a jokey picture of whisky drinkers from Scotland

indicators.note: drinking takes something inside, so one piece goes within another
a drop is a tiny amount, here just one opening letter

blocks.note: sots are habitual drinkers
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Boozers knock back a dram of Scotch from Caledonia.
explanation.walkthrough: Caledonian is a brewery and also the old Latin name for Scottish, which is why the whole clue doubles as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Natives of Scotland, pictured fondly as whisky drinkers, are people from Caledonia, the Roman name for that country.

clue.text: Architectural feature on Odeon I'm converting

indicators.note: to convert is to change form, so the letters are remade

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone remodelling an Odeon cinema adds a bit of decorative architecture.
explanation.walkthrough: The Odeon is a British cinema chain whose buildings are known for distinctive architecture, which makes the surface plausible.
explanation.definitionFit: A bulbous rooftop cupola, typical of Russian churches, is one type of feature in building design.

clue.text: One having three lines listened to stoned fancy

indicators.note: something listened to is heard rather than read, so its sound matters

blocks.note: stoned is high, and coo is an exclamation like fancy that

explanation.surface: Someone who has smoked something imagines they have heard a fanciful idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coo' and 'fancy!' are both old British exclamations of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: This Japanese verse form is made of a short three-part structure, so it is one with three lines.

clue.text: Just starting nice pint (I must get trashed)

indicators.note: something trashed is wrecked and jumbled into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, joining the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A drinker at the start of a night out vows to get wasted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trashed' is British slang for very drunk, which fits the pint in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Incipient describes something in an early stage, beginning to happen or develop.

clue.text: People often found in The Den ogling wingers?

definitions.text: People often found in The Den ogling wingers?

blocks.clueFragment: People often found in The Den ogling wingers?
blocks.note: surface reading: football fans at Millwall's ground eyeing the wide players
setter's reading: keen birders sitting in a hide watching creatures with wings

explanation.surface: Millwall supporters at their home ground watch the wide players closely.
explanation.walkthrough: The Den is the ground of Millwall football club in London, and wingers are attacking wide players; here a den is a hide and wingers are birds.
explanation.definitionFit: Obsessive birdwatchers who rush to see rare species are known by this British term and spend hours in hides.

clue.text: Actors like being around ten flipping clappers

indicators.note: to be around something is to surround it
flipping something turns it over end to end

blocks.note: the cast is the set of actors in a show
like and as both mean in the manner of
taken as written

explanation.surface: Performers seem to be applauding wildly, as if surrounded by ten frantic fans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British curse; it is the turnaround signal.
explanation.definitionFit: These wooden shells are struck together in the hand to make a clicking sound, so they are percussion clappers.

clue.text: Turning red if Celia throws a paddy

indicators.note: to throw something is to cast it away, so a letter is discarded
turning things around changes their order

blocks.note: taken as written
the single letter that is thrown out

explanation.surface: Celia goes red in the face when she throws a tantrum.
explanation.walkthrough: A paddy is British slang for a temper tantrum, but the definition is the other paddy, a flooded field.
explanation.definitionFit: A paddy is a flooded field where rice is grown, so the two terms are synonyms.

clue.text: Say love is nursing street people with swollen heads

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold close, cradling something inside

blocks.note: e.g. means for example, say
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O
taken as written
ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: Love is caring for homeless people with injuries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swollen heads' sounds medical; it means conceit.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-centred individuals who think too much of themselves are said to have big heads, so they fit.

clue.text: Merit editor's upset and be a man!

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so read bottom to top

blocks.note: ED is the usual abbreviation for editor
the men are the ordinary troops, so being one is to serve

explanation.surface: An editor is upset over praise and is told to toughen up.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', joining editor to its signal. 'Be a man!' sounds like an order to toughen up; it means to do service in the ranks.
explanation.definitionFit: To merit something is to be worthy of it, which is what this verb means.

clue.text: One in Red Dwarf perhaps getting a step up?

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
a red dwarf is a small cool type of star

explanation.surface: A character in the TV sitcom Red Dwarf wins a promotion.
explanation.walkthrough: Red Dwarf is a British sci-fi sitcom, but here it is the astronomical object; 'perhaps' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A single tread on a staircase lets you climb, so it is literally one step up.

clue.text: Haughty Hoskins is dangerous, but not ultimately evil

indicators.note: not means without, so something is removed
ultimately means in the end, pointing to a final letter

blocks.note: the setter is speaking of himself: I am, shortened
full of peril
the final letter of the word, to be removed

explanation.surface: A self-mocking claim that the setter is arrogant and menacing, though not truly wicked.
explanation.walkthrough: Hoskins is the setter's pseudonym, so 'Hoskins is' is the setter saying I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: Imperious means domineering and arrogant, acting like an emperor, a close synonym of haughty.

clue.text: Search hard around south for a place to sleep

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: to root is to rummage and dig about
S is the abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: A traveller hunts high and low in the south for a bed for the night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Search hard' is a single unit meaning to rummage, like a pig rooting.
explanation.definitionFit: A roost is a perch where birds settle at night, hence somewhere to rest and sleep.

clue.text: A setter enthralling foremost of newspapers?

definitions.text: A setter enthralling foremost of newspapers?
definitions.note: the whole clue: a delightful compiler is a heavenly being

indicators.note: to enthral is to hold captive, keeping something within
the foremost part of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: taken as written
gel is something that sets
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A crossword compiler captivates newspaper readers.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter is the usual word for a crossword compiler, but here it is something that sets, a jelly; the question mark admits the whole clue is a fond, self-praising definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A delightful, kindly person is called a darling or saint, so a setter who charms readers earns that heavenly name.

clue.text: Emerald, perhaps one with a hole in it?

definitions.text: one with a hole in it

blocks.note: first meaning: a bright colour like that of the gemstone

blocks.clueFragment: one with a hole in it
blocks.note: second meaning: the putting surface around each flag on a golf course

explanation.walkthrough: 'One with a hole in it' suggests something damaged; on a golf course every putting surface has a hole.
explanation.definitionFit: Emerald is a shade of the colour, and every golf putting surface contains the cup.

clue.text: With smells around, smell trainers?

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: to reek is to stink
BO is body odour

explanation.surface: Smelly sports shoes give off an odour all around.
explanation.walkthrough: Trainers is the British word for sneakers; Reeboks are a brand of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Reeboks are a well-known brand of athletic shoe, so they are examples of trainers.

clue.text: Joints engineers knocked back in Sandbanks

indicators.note: knocked back means sent backwards, so the letters run the other way
in places one thing inside another

blocks.note: reefs are ridges of sand or rock near the surface
RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps

explanation.surface: Engineers down drinks in Sandbanks, a wealthy resort on the Dorset coast.
explanation.walkthrough: Sandbanks is a rich seaside spot in southern England, but here it is just sandbanks; 'knocked back' looks like drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: Reefer is slang for a cannabis cigarette, and a joint is the same thing.

clue.text: Might you say American as Barack Obama?

blocks.note: first meaning, cryptic: someone from the States, split into two words
second meaning: a distinguished political leader

explanation.surface: A question about whether a former US president counts as typically American.
explanation.walkthrough: The States is a common name for the USA, so a person from there is an American.
explanation.definitionFit: Obama is a respected senior political figure, an example of a gender-neutral word for a statesman.
